newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE - U.S. holding the line against immigration.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. holding the line against immigration.

text.p: Here on the border between the First and the Third worlds, the price of the American Dream has risen steeply for poor immigrants.

For many Mexicans, crossing the border into California used to be a whimsical dash in search of a better life. The consequences of failure were a few hours in the custody of the U.S. Border Patrol and a free bus ride back to Tijuana.

Now, a 10-foot (three-metre)-high metal wall stands in the way. Behind that is a phalanx of border patrol agents armed with floodlights, night-vision telescopes, sensors to detect ground movements, dogs, horses, motorcycles, four-wheel-drive vehicles and other manhunting tools.
"It looks like a war scene," said Victor Clark Alfaro, a human rights activist from Tijuana who has made the border his life's study.

The crackdown has pushed illegal immigrant routes further east through the treacherous Otay Mountains, where 29 people died of accidents or exposure in 1996. Smugglers have jacked up rates for providing safe passage, further squeezing poor would-be migrants.

It all started with Operation Gatekeeper, the U.S. Border Patrol's 2-year-old programme to stem the tide of illegal immigration from Tijuana to San Diego, an area accounting for a third of illegal migrant crossings. Similar operations -- called Safeguard in Tucson, Arizona, and Hold the Line in El Paso, Texas -- also have been effective in stemming the tide along the 2,000-mile (3,000-km) border).
THE FENCE IS WORKING

Gatekeeper was the U.S. government's response to rising concern about illegal immigration in vote-rich California. And from all indications it is working; statistics back up what experts on both sides of the border say -- that fewer people are attempting to cross into San Diego. Apprehensions by the Border Patrol in the San Diego Sector fell about eight percent to 483,815 in the last fiscal year, down from 524,231 in 1995.

"I think everyone agrees we're more effective. I would attribute the decrease to our higher profile. It's a different way to operate but in my opinion it's the only way to operate," Ron Henley, a 12-year veteran of the sector, said.

Elsewhere, success is measured by a sharp increase in apprehensions as the crackdown in San Diego pushes illegal immigration routes not just to the Otay Mountains but further east to Arizona and Texas as well. For the 1996 fiscal year, total U.S. arrests of illegal immigrants rose 13.8 percent to 1,507,270 from 1,324,202 in 1995. In El Paso, they increased 31.5 percent, while Tucson's haul was up 34.7 percent.
More than 97 percent of those caught are Mexicans.

Since Operation Gatekeeper was announced on Oct. 2, 1994, Washington has sent 700 more border agents to San Diego, for a total of 1,955. Disciplined and well-supervised units now have smaller stretches of border to guard.

They are helped by 14-mile (22-km)-long solid metal fence from the Pacific Ocean inland. As a result, many would-be immigrants are bottled up in Tijuana, surrounded by soaring drug-related violence and grinding poverty.
"PEOPLE ARE FRUSTRATED ... DESPERATE"

"People are frustrated, spent, desperate," Clark, director of the Binational Centre for Human Rights, told Reuters. "They don't have much money in their pockets when they get to Tijuana. The levels of social tension are a lot higher."

On peak days the Border Patrol deports up to 1,800 Mexicans to Tijuana, dropping them off at the border. According to Tijuana Police Chief Jorge Alvarez Barriere, 1,500 of them try to cross again the next day, 100 return to their hometowns and 200 make a new home in Tijuana.

Luis Herrera-Lasso, the Mexican consul general in San Diego, said 38 Mexicans died on the U.S. side while in transit last year, 29 of them in the Otay Mountains. So far in 1997, there have been 14 deaths north of the border, mostly due to hypothermia from unusually cold weather.

"It's one of the major concerns that I have today," he told Reuters. "The mountains are 4,000 feet (1,200 metres) high, there are extreme temperatures, there's no water, there's no food and it's three to five days on foot before you get to a road."
As a result, one smuggler called Jose Luis said he is charging $800 to $1,000 for a full-service trip from Tijuana to Los Angeles, up from $200 to $400 a few years ago.

"It's a lot more difficult transporting illegals through the mountains," he told Reuters from Tijuana's North Zone, a patchwork of bars and brothels where immigrants -- pollos, or chickens, they are called -- meet their escorts ("coyotes").
"It's a lot riskier walking for three days through slopes, scrubland and canyons, where all the bands of criminals are hiding out."
